title: King's Indian: each side's setup and what each move prepares
outcomes: Says, for Black's first five moves in the King's Indian (Nf6, g6, Bg7, d6, O-O), what each prepares, and why ...e5 before castling loses a pawn
Recognises four White set-ups (Classical, Fianchetto, Sämisch, Four Pawns) from the pawns and bishops and names one idea of each
Counts attackers and defenders before capturing on e4 and sees why ...Nxe4 loses a piece for a pawn
Knows that different move orders can reach the same position, and reads opening counts as results of games, not verdicts

steps.text: **The question of this lesson.** Every early move does two jobs: it stands somewhere, and it makes a later move possible. By the end you will say, for the first moves of each side, what the move prepares. You will also recognise four White set-ups (Classical, Fianchetto, Sämisch, Four Pawns) and show one position where skipping a preparing move costs a pawn. Marks: [V] checked here, [I] inference, [H] hypothesis.

steps.text: **Castling first is what makes ...e5 possible.** The count on e5 is the same in both lines: two attackers, one defender. With the king on g8, though, Black has a shot: after Nxe5, ...Nxe4! and ...Bxe5 regain the pawn. With the king on d8, the same shot meets Bg5+ and fails [V]. Condition: the shot needs the king off d8. Before a strike in the centre, ask where each king would stand if the queens vanished.

steps.text: **What each set-up gives and gives up.** [I] Classical: simple development, castle early, and a choice about d4 at move seven. Fianchetto: the bishop eyes the long diagonal and the e-pawn often waits until the king is safe. Sämisch: a firm e4 and an attack plan, but slow on the kingside. Four Pawns: the most space, the most targets. [H] Their strength differs less than the kind of game they ask of Black; the engine scores are all close.

steps.text: **A habit from this lesson.** Before you take a pawn, count: how many of my pieces attack it, how many of theirs defend it, and what recaptures. Black's knight on f6 attacks e4 in every set-up above, and in the Classical, Sämisch and Four Pawns set-ups the pawn is defended. Equal counts still lose if your capturing piece is worth more than the pawn. [H] This may be a common way to lose material here; we have not counted it.

**Test yourself.** Three new positions follow. Nobody says which set-up it is, and nobody says what the last move prepares. Decide first from the pawns and the bishops, then check. A set-up is recognised by its signs, not by whether e4 has been played yet.

**Recap: what to remember.** Black's early moves are preparations: the knight and the pawn on g6 make room for the bishop, the pawn on d6 guards e5, castling puts the king beyond the queen trade. White chooses a set-up with the fifth move: Classical, Fianchetto, Sämisch or Four Pawns. Different move orders can reach the same position. Before taking a pawn, count attackers and defenders. Next lesson: the Classical main line, move by move.
